**Night Owl’s Guide to Blue-Light Filtering Software: Comfort for Your Eyes After Dark**  

For many of us, laptops have become our constant companions, accompanying us through long workdays and late-night creative sessions. While productivity may thrive under the glow of a screen, our eyes are often the silent victims of extended digital exposure—especially at night. One of the most effective ways to reduce nighttime eye strain is the use of blue-light filtering software. This post explores why blue-light filtering matters, compares leading applications, and examines how customization can make a real difference in your comfort and sleep quality.  

---

### Why Blue-Light Filtering Matters  

Digital displays emit a significant amount of blue light, a high-energy wavelength that can contribute to visual fatigue, headaches, and disruption of the body’s circadian rhythm. At night, when ambient lighting is lower, blue light’s intensity can feel harsher, making sustained focus more difficult and potentially interfering with melatonin production. Over time, repeated exposure in these conditions can leave eyes feeling dry, strained, and sensitive.  

Blue-light filtering software addresses this by altering the color temperature of your screen, shifting it from cooler, bluish tones to warmer, amber hues. This subtle change can make prolonged nighttime use more comfortable and help prepare your body for rest.  

---

### Comparing Popular Applications  

Several tools are available to help manage blue-light exposure, each with its own strengths:  

**f.lux**  
One of the earliest and most widely used solutions, f.lux automatically adjusts your screen’s color temperature based on your location and time of day. It offers smooth transitions between day and night modes, and allows manual overrides for specific tasks that require accurate color rendering. The interface is straightforward, making it a good choice for users who want a “set it and forget it” experience.  

**Windows Night Light / macOS Night Shift**  
Both Windows and macOS now include built-in blue-light reduction features. While these may lack the advanced scheduling and fine-tuning options of third-party software, they integrate seamlessly into the operating system and require no extra installation. They’re ideal for users who want simplicity and minimal configuration.  

**Iris**  
A more feature-rich option, Iris offers granular control over brightness, color temperature, and even screen flicker reduction. It includes modes tailored for reading, programming, or movie watching, making it versatile for different nighttime activities. Iris also supports automation, so you can set specific parameters for different times of day or ambient light conditions.  

---

### The Power of Customization  

Customization is key to maximizing the benefits of blue-light filtering. While default settings can help, every user’s eyes and environment are different. Factors such as the position of your screen, the brightness of your workspace, and your sensitivity to color shifts all influence the optimal configuration.  

For example, some users find that a gradual transition from daylight settings to warmer tones over 30–60 minutes is less jarring and more comfortable than an abrupt change. Others may prefer a stronger reduction in blue light during late-night hours, especially if they work in dimly lit rooms.  

Advanced applications like Iris or f.lux allow you to fine-tune these transitions, choose exact color temperatures (e.g., 3400K for a deep amber effect), and even set profiles for specific tasks. Experimenting with these settings can help you strike a balance between visual comfort and accurate color representation.  

---

### Additional Tips for Nighttime Comfort  

Blue-light filtering is most effective when combined with other healthy screen habits. Adjusting screen brightness to match your environment, maintaining a proper viewing distance, and taking short breaks every 20–30 minutes can all reduce strain. If you work late into the night, consider dimming surrounding lights and using warmer bulbs to complement your on-screen adjustments.  

---

### Final Thoughts  

Blue-light filtering software has evolved from a niche utility into a mainstream tool for protecting eye health during nighttime laptop use. Whether you opt for built-in OS features or more advanced third-party solutions, the key lies in finding the right balance of warmth, brightness, and transition timing for your needs. With the right configuration, you can make your late-night sessions more comfortable, preserve your focus, and support your body’s natural rhythms—without sacrificing productivity or enjoyment.  

By exploring the options and customizing them to your environment, your eyes will thank you for every amber-hued hour you spend working or unwinding after dark.

**Reading the Fire: How to Judge Your Wood Stove’s Efficiency by Flame Color and Pattern**  

When you spend time in front of a wood-burning stove, you quickly learn that the flames are more than just a visual pleasure—they are a living indicator of how well your stove is performing. By training your eye to notice subtle differences in flame coloration and movement, you can gain valuable insight into combustion efficiency, heat output, and whether adjustments to your airflow settings are needed.  

---

### Understanding Flame Color as a Combustion Indicator  

One of the most immediate clues to a stove’s performance is the hue of the flames. In general terms:  

- **Bright yellow-orange flames** often indicate a healthy, hot burn with sufficient oxygen, especially when they are lively and clean-edged.  
- **Dull, sooty orange or reddish flames** may point to incomplete combustion, often caused by restricted air supply or overly damp fuel.  
- **Blue or bluish-violet flames** can appear when volatile gases are burning efficiently, sometimes more visible during the early stages of combustion or when the stove is running very hot.  

If you see persistent dark orange or red tones accompanied by visible smoke from the chimney, it’s a sign that unburned particulates are escaping—meaning you’re losing potential heat energy and contributing to creosote buildup in the flue.  

---

### The Role of Flame Shape and Movement  

Color tells part of the story; the way flames move tells the rest. In an efficient burn:  

- Flames should be **active but not chaotic**, rising steadily without excessive flickering.  
- The firebed should glow evenly, with smaller tongues of flame dancing above it rather than large, lazy billows.  
- When air is well-balanced, flames tend to be shorter and sharper, indicating that gases are combusting quickly and completely.  

In contrast, long, rolling flames that appear to “search” for oxygen may suggest the stove is starved for air. This can occur if the air vents are too restricted or if ash buildup is impeding airflow through the grate.  

---

### Airflow Adjustments for Better Combustion  

Most wood stoves allow you to control primary and secondary air supplies. Learning to fine-tune these inputs can significantly improve performance:  

- **Primary air** feeds the base of the fire and is crucial for igniting fresh fuel loads. Too much primary air over time, however, can cause excessive heat loss up the flue.  
- **Secondary air** is introduced above the firebed, helping ignite gases released from the wood. Proper use of secondary air often leads to cleaner flames and reduced smoke.  

A good practice is to open the air controls more during ignition or refueling to establish a robust burn, then gradually reduce airflow to maintain steady heat without over-fueling the flames. Watching for a shift from smoky, lazy flames to bright, steady ones is your visual cue that you’ve reached an optimal setting.  

---

### Fuel Quality and Its Impact on Flame Behavior  

Even perfect airflow can’t overcome poor-quality fuel. Wood that is too damp will produce cooler, smokier flames, often with a dull orange cast and sluggish movement. Properly seasoned wood—generally dried for at least 6–12 months—burns hotter, with brighter flames and less visible smoke.  

Hardwoods tend to produce longer-lasting coals and more stable flames, while softwoods ignite quickly and can produce more vigorous early flames but shorter burn times. Observing how the flames behave with different fuel types can help you choose the right balance for your heating needs.  

---

### Using Visual Feedback to Maximize Heat Output  

By combining observations of flame color, shape, and movement, you can make small, informed tweaks to your stove operation that add up to noticeable improvements in heat output and fuel economy. Over time, you’ll develop an intuitive sense of when your stove is running at peak efficiency—often without needing to check thermometers or other instruments.  

A bright, lively flame with minimal smoke is more than just beautiful; it’s a sign that you’re getting the most warmth from every log, reducing waste, and keeping your chimney cleaner. In the long run, this means less fuel consumed, fewer maintenance issues, and a more comfortable home.  

---

**In essence:** your wood stove’s flames are a direct reflection of the combustion process. By learning to read their color and behavior, you can make real-time adjustments to improve efficiency and enjoy a cleaner, hotter, and more satisfying fire.

# 2.0 Need for Crack Treatment If a particular cracked pavement appears to be in need of some sort of maintenance, a relatively quick assessment can be made to ascertain the need and, more importantly, to help in determining the appropriate action. Such an assessment requires an evaluation of existing pavement conditions and a knowledge of future rehabilitation plans, both of which may be found in a pavement management system (PMS). # 2.1 Pavement/Crack Evaluation Although maintenance engineers or supervisors are normally quite familiar with the roads they maintain, a quick review of construction, maintenance, and other records will provide important general information regarding the following: ! Pavement age. ! Pavement and geometric design. ! Pavement section boundaries. ! Traffic. ! Climate. ! Type and extent of previous maintenance treatments. 1 Condition rating. After these records are reviewed, a shoulder survey should then be performed on a small representative sample of the pavement section, about $150 \mathrm{~m}$, to determine the amount, type, and condition or severity of cracks, as well as the condition or effectiveness of any previously applied crack treatments (see section 5.0). A sample survey form for recording pavement and crack information is provided in figure 1. Figure 1. Asphalt pavement/crack survey form. # 2.2 Determining the Type of Maintenance The appropriate type of maintenance for cracked pavements often depends on the density and general condition of the cracks. If cracks are abundant and do not exhibit a high degree of edge deterioration, they may best be treated through chip seals, slurry seals, or the like. If cracks are low to moderate in density and have typically progressed to a point of high edge deterioration, then crack repair strategies, such as partial-depth patching or spot patching, may be warranted. If cracks are moderate in density and show moderate to no deterioration at the edges, then they may be treated effectively through sealing or filling operations. Table 2 summarizes these guidelines. As table 2 indicates, crack density levels are described in general terms. This is because experienced personnel can make reasonable assessments of density. Figures 2 through 5 illustrate typical crack situations and potential remedies. Table 2. Guidelines for determining the type of maintenance to be performed. | | | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Crack Density | Average Level of Edge Deterioration (percentage of crack length) | | Low (0 to 25) | Moderate (26 to 50) | High (51 to 100) | | Low | Nothing | Nothing or Crack Treatment | Crack Repair | | Moderate | Crack Treatment | Crack Treatment | Crack Repair | | High | Surface Treatment | Surface Treatment | Rehabilitation | Figure 2. Pavement candidate for surface treatment: high-density cracking. Figure 3. Pavement candidate for crack repair. Figure 4. Pavement candidate for transverse crack sealing. Figure 5. Pavement candidate for longitudinal crack filling. In general, a large number of cracks or severely deteriorated cracks indicate a pavement in an advanced state of decay. Crack sealing or filling in these circumstances is both uneconomical and technically unsound, as it does little to delay the need for more extensive corrective actions. Most highway agencies have established policies that specify the type of maintenance to be performed on cracked pavements and when to perform it. The policies are often based on an assessment of the overall pavement condition (extent of cracking) or specific crack characteristics (type and width). # 2.2.1 Other Considerations On occasion, cracks may have other types of deficiencies. In particular, crack edges may exhibit vertical distresses, such as cupping, lipping, or faulting, or may undergo significant vertical deflections or movements under traffic loading. Such deficiencies can add significantly to overall pavement roughness and can deteriorate rapidly. Normally, repair alternatives such as patching or milling are appropriate for correcting these deficiencies. However, if the amount of vertical deflection and the severity of the distress are not too high, a temporary fix with crack treatment may be adequate. # 2.3 Objectives of Sealing and Filling Although little distinction has been made in the past between crack sealing and crack filling, the purposes and functions of each must be clearly understood so that the most cost-effective and long-lasting treatment is applied. Crack Sealing— The placement of specialized treatment materials above or into working cracks using unique configurations to prevent the intrusion of water and incompressibles into the crack. Crack Filling— The placement of ordinary treatment materials into non-working cracks to substantially reduce infiltration of water and to reinforce the adjacent pavement. As these definitions indicate, the objectives of crack sealing are significantly more difficult to accomplish than those of crack filling. Sealing requires considerably more forethought, greater costs, and the use of more specially formulated materials and more sophisticated equipment. It is assumed in this manual that where cracks are exhibiting significant vertical deflections, the appropriate repair strategy will be sought. Hence, for cracks with limited vertical movement, horizontal movement becomes the critical factor in determining the need for, and planning of, a crack treatment operation.

Recycled paper processing mills use paper as their feedstock. The recovered
paper is combined with water in a large vessel called a pulper that acts like
a blender to separate fibers in the paper sheets from each other. The
resultant slurry then passes through screens and other separation processes to
remove contaminants such as ink, clays, dirt, plastic and metals. The amount
of contaminants that are acceptable in the pulp depends upon the type of paper
being produced. Mechanical separation equipment includes coarse and fine
screens, centrifugal cleaners, and dispersion or kneading units that break
apart ink particles. Deinking processes use special systems aided by soaps or
surfactants to wash or float ink and other particles away from the fiber.

**Innovations in Biodegradable Packaging Materials from Plant-Based Sources: Production, Decomposition, and Market Adoption**

**Abstract**  
The increasing environmental burden of synthetic polymer packaging has prompted significant research into biodegradable alternatives derived from plant-based feedstocks. This paper examines recent advances in the development and commercialization of such materials, with emphasis on production methodologies, decomposition behavior in industrial composting environments, and factors influencing market adoption. Data from laboratory trials and pilot-scale composting facilities are reviewed to assess degradation rates, residual impacts, and scalability. The findings suggest that while plant-based biodegradable packaging demonstrates promising environmental performance, economic and infrastructural challenges remain in achieving widespread substitution for conventional plastics.

**1. Introduction**  
Packaging waste constitutes a substantial proportion of municipal solid waste streams, with synthetic polymers exhibiting persistence in terrestrial and marine environments [1]. Biodegradable packaging materials sourced from renewable plant-based inputs—such as starch, cellulose, polylactic acid (PLA), and polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs)—offer a potential pathway toward reducing long-term ecological impacts. The transition to these materials requires not only technological innovation in production processes but also assurance of effective end-of-life degradation under realistic waste management conditions. This paper synthesizes recent developments in plant-based biodegradable packaging, focusing on the interface between material science and waste treatment infrastructure.

**2. Production of Plant-Based Biodegradable Packaging**  
Plant-based packaging materials are typically produced by extracting polysaccharides or fermenting plant-derived sugars into biopolymers. Starch-based films, for example, are created through gelatinization and blending with plasticizers to improve flexibility [2]. PLA is produced via the polymerization of lactic acid, itself obtained through the fermentation of corn or sugarcane feedstocks. PHAs are synthesized by certain bacterial strains utilizing plant oils or sugars as substrates. Advances in compounding techniques have enabled the incorporation of reinforcing fibers, nanocellulose, or biodegradable additives to enhance mechanical performance and moisture resistance. However, feedstock sourcing raises considerations of agricultural land use, water consumption, and potential competition with food production, necessitating life cycle assessments to fully evaluate environmental trade-offs.

**3. Decomposition in Composting Facilities**  
The biodegradation of plant-based packaging materials depends on environmental conditions, particularly temperature, humidity, and microbial activity. Industrial composting facilities, operating at thermophilic temperatures (50–70°C), provide optimal conditions for microbial hydrolysis and assimilation of biopolymers. PLA typically achieves >90% mass loss within 60–90 days under such conditions [3], whereas starch-based films may degrade more rapidly, often within 30–45 days. PHAs exhibit high biodegradability across a range of conditions, including marine environments, though degradation rates are slower in lower-temperature composting. Residual fragments are generally minimal when process parameters are maintained, reducing the risk of environmental persistence. Nevertheless, contamination with non-compostable materials can hinder processing efficiency and final compost quality.

**4. Market Adoption Factors**  
Despite technical viability, market penetration of plant-based biodegradable packaging remains limited by several factors. Cost parity with conventional plastics has not yet been achieved at scale, though increased production capacity and feedstock diversification may narrow the gap. Regulatory frameworks mandating compostable packaging in specific sectors have spurred adoption in regions with robust composting infrastructure. Consumer perception also plays a role; clear labeling and education on proper disposal pathways influence end-user compliance. A critical barrier is the mismatch between material design and local waste management capabilities—municipalities lacking industrial composting facilities may inadvertently direct biodegradable packaging to landfills, where anaerobic conditions slow degradation and can lead to methane emissions [4].

**5. Conclusion**  
Plant-based biodegradable packaging materials present a viable alternative to petroleum-derived plastics in reducing environmental persistence of packaging waste. Advances in production science have improved mechanical properties and reduced costs, while composting trials confirm rapid decomposition under controlled thermophilic conditions. To realize their potential, coordinated efforts among material scientists, waste management authorities, policymakers, and industry stakeholders are required to align product design with disposal infrastructure. Future research should focus on optimizing feedstock utilization, lowering production energy inputs, and enhancing biodegradation under diverse environmental contexts.

**Title:**  
Seasonal Variability and Crop Performance: Consequences of an Absent Spring Period in Agricultural Systems  

**Abstract**  
Seasonal transitions play a critical role in determining agricultural productivity, particularly through their influence on planting schedules, crop development, and yield outcomes. This paper examines the agronomic implications of climates where a distinct spring season is absent or significantly compressed. Drawing from climatological data and agronomic studies, we analyze how the lack of a gradual transition from winter to summer affects soil preparation, germination rates, pest cycles, and the synchronization of crop phenology. The findings highlight the necessity of adaptive management strategies, including cultivar selection, modified sowing times, and integrated pest control, to mitigate yield losses in regions affected by abrupt seasonal changes.  

**1. Introduction**  
Seasonal changes form the backbone of traditional agricultural calendars. In temperate regions, spring serves as a critical intermediary phase, allowing gradual warming, increased daylight, and moderated precipitation patterns that collectively support optimal planting and early growth stages [1]. However, in certain climates—such as those influenced by continental extremes or rapid shifts due to climate change—the spring period may be truncated or absent, with temperatures transitioning rapidly from winter cold to summer heat. This absence can disrupt established agricultural practices, necessitating a re-evaluation of planting schedules and crop management protocols.  

**2. Climatic Context and the Absence of Spring**  
Regions lacking a defined spring often experience prolonged winters followed by an abrupt onset of high temperatures. This phenomenon can be observed in parts of Central Asia, interior North America, and certain high-altitude zones [2]. The rapid shift in temperature and photoperiod compresses the window for soil thawing, nutrient cycling, and seedbed preparation. Additionally, precipitation patterns may be misaligned with crop water requirements, as snowmelt overlaps with the early stages of heat stress rather than supporting gradual growth.  

**3. Impact on Planting Schedules**  
In conventional temperate agriculture, spring provides a predictable period for sowing cool-season crops such as wheat, barley, and certain legumes. Without this transitional phase, farmers must either plant earlier during sub-optimal soil temperatures or delay until summer warmth, risking exposure to heat stress during critical growth phases [3]. Early planting in frozen or waterlogged soils can lead to poor germination, while delayed planting compresses the growing season, affecting yield potential.  

**4. Crop Development and Phenological Mismatch**  
The absence of a gradual spring transition can cause phenological mismatches between crop development stages and environmental conditions. For example, crops that rely on vernalization may complete cold exposure prematurely, initiating flowering before sufficient vegetative growth has occurred [4]. The shortened cool period also affects root establishment and nutrient uptake, making crops more vulnerable to summer droughts and pests.  

**5. Pest and Disease Dynamics**  
Pest emergence and pathogen proliferation are closely tied to seasonal temperature patterns. A rapid shift from winter to summer can disrupt established cycles, leading to either an overlap of pest activity with vulnerable crop stages or the emergence of novel pest pressures [5]. In some cases, beneficial insect populations may be reduced due to the loss of intermediate temperatures that support their life cycles, further destabilizing pest control dynamics.  

**6. Adaptive Strategies**  
Mitigation of yield losses in regions without a defined spring requires targeted interventions. Farmers may adopt heat-tolerant or early-maturing cultivars to align crop phenology with prevailing conditions. Adjustments to irrigation scheduling, use of mulches to moderate soil temperature, and staggered planting dates can also reduce risk. Integrating weather forecasting tools and phenology models improves decision-making, allowing for more precise timing of sowing and input application.  

**7. Conclusion**  
The absence of a distinct spring season presents unique challenges for agricultural systems, disrupting conventional planting schedules, crop development, and pest management. Understanding the climatic drivers behind these changes and implementing adaptive strategies is essential for sustaining productivity in affected regions. Future research should focus on breeding programs for resilience to compressed seasonal transitions and on refining predictive models to support farmers under evolving climatic conditions.

[2] Chen, L., et al. (2017). Climatic extremes and agricultural adaptation in continental interiors. *Climate Research*, 72(3), 215–228.  
[3] Patel, R., & Johnson, M. (2018). Sowing date optimization under variable seasonal conditions. *Field Crops Research*, 220, 10–19.  
[4] Huang, Y., & Gomez, P. (2019). Vernalization responses in cereals under changing climates. *Plant Physiology Reports*, 24(1), 33–42.

**Report: Comparative Analysis of Chlorine-Free Swimming Pool Sanitation Methods**  

---

**Abstract**  
This report examines alternative swimming pool sanitation methods that eliminate the use of chlorine as a primary disinfectant. It compares ozone treatment systems, saltwater chlorination, and other non-chlorine technologies, analyzing their relative health impacts, cost considerations, and maintenance requirements. The discussion aims to provide pool owners, facility managers, and public health authorities with a detailed understanding of the practical benefits and limitations associated with chlorine-free sanitation approaches.  

---

**1. Introduction**  
Chlorine has been the dominant disinfectant in swimming pools for decades due to its proven efficacy in eliminating pathogens and preventing waterborne illnesses. However, concerns about chemical exposure, skin and eye irritation, and environmental impact have driven interest in chlorine-free alternatives. This report explores three major categories of non-chlorine sanitation: ozone treatment, saltwater systems (which generate chlorine from salt but reduce the need for direct chlorine addition), and other emerging technologies such as UV treatment and mineral-based filtration.  

---

**2. Ozone Treatment Systems**  

**2.1 Principle of Operation**  
Ozone (O₃) is a powerful oxidizing agent that destroys bacteria, viruses, and organic contaminants through oxidation. In pool applications, ozone is generated onsite using an ozone generator and injected into the water circulation system.  

**2.2 Health Implications**  
Ozone treatment reduces the presence of chloramines, which are responsible for much of the irritation associated with traditional chlorination. Because ozone rapidly decomposes back into oxygen, residual chemical exposure to swimmers is minimal. However, ozone gas must be carefully contained to prevent inhalation risks.  

**2.3 Cost and Maintenance**  
Initial installation costs for ozone systems are generally higher than for conventional chlorination, often ranging from $5,000 to $8,000 for large pools. Maintenance involves periodic inspection and replacement of generator components, with operational costs tied to electricity consumption.  

---

**3. Saltwater Systems**  

**3.1 Principle of Operation**  
Saltwater pools use electrolysis to convert dissolved salt into chlorine, which sanitizes the water. While technically chlorine is still present, the process avoids direct addition of concentrated chemical products.  

**3.2 Health Implications**  
Saltwater systems typically maintain lower chlorine concentrations than traditional pools, reducing skin and eye irritation. The softer feel of the water and absence of strong chlorine odor are often cited as advantages for swimmer comfort.  

**3.3 Cost and Maintenance**  
Installation costs for saltwater chlorinators range from $1,500 to $3,000. Maintenance includes periodic cleaning of the electrolytic cell and monitoring salt levels. Equipment lifespan is typically five to seven years, with replacement costs factored into long-term budgeting.  

---

**4. Other Non-Chlorine Technologies**  

**4.1 Ultraviolet (UV) Treatment**  
UV systems disinfect water by exposing it to ultraviolet light, which disrupts the DNA of microorganisms. While effective for pathogen control, UV does not provide residual sanitation, requiring integration with other low-level disinfectants.  

**4.2 Mineral-Based Filtration**  
Certain systems use silver or copper ions to inhibit microbial growth. These approaches are supplementary and often require combination with other methods to ensure full pathogen eradication.  

---

**5. Comparative Analysis**  

| Method             | Health Benefits                 | Cost Range        | Maintenance Level | Residual Protection |
|--------------------|---------------------------------|-------------------|-------------------|---------------------|
| Ozone Treatment    | Minimal chemical exposure; reduced chloramines | High ($5k–$8k)     | Moderate           | Low (requires backup) |
| Saltwater System   | Softer water; reduced irritation | Medium ($1.5k–$3k)| Moderate           | High (chlorine present) |
| UV Treatment       | No chemical exposure             | Medium ($2k–$4k)  | Low to Moderate   | None (requires backup) |
| Mineral Filtration | Low chemical exposure            | Low to Medium     | Low               | Low                 |

---

**6. Conclusion**  
Chlorine-free or reduced-chlorine swimming pool sanitation methods present viable alternatives to conventional chemical disinfection, offering improved swimmer comfort and reduced environmental impact. Ozone treatment excels in minimizing chemical exposure but demands higher capital investment and supplemental sanitation. Saltwater systems offer a balance between comfort and residual protection, though they still rely on chlorine generated from salt. UV and mineral-based systems serve as effective supplementary technologies but require integration with other sanitizing methods for comprehensive protection.  

For decision-makers, the choice among these options should consider budget constraints, desired health outcomes, maintenance capacity, and regulatory compliance. Continued innovation in non-chlorine technologies may further expand feasible options for maintaining safe and enjoyable swimming environments without reliance on traditional chlorine dosing.

**Perennial Crops in Mediterranean Agriculture: Grapes and Olives**  

In Mediterranean climates, the cultivation of perennial crops has played a central role in agricultural systems for millennia. Among these, grapes (*Vitis vinifera*) and olives (*Olea europaea*) are particularly notable, both for their economic significance and their deep integration into the culinary traditions of the region. Their adaptation to the specific environmental conditions of the Mediterranean basin—characterized by hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters—has ensured their persistence as cornerstone crops from antiquity to the present day.  

**Historical Background**  
Archaeological evidence indicates that grape cultivation in the Mediterranean dates back at least to the Neolithic period, with domestication occurring in the Near East before spreading westward along trade and migration routes. By the Bronze Age, viticulture was firmly established in regions such as Greece, Italy, and the Levant. Olives, similarly, have a documented history of cultivation extending over 6,000 years, with early centers in the eastern Mediterranean. Both crops were not only staples of diet but also integral to trade networks, with olive oil and wine serving as high-value commodities exchanged across the ancient world.  

**Environmental Adaptations**  
Grapes and olives share several traits that make them well-suited to Mediterranean climates. Both species are drought-tolerant once established, with deep root systems capable of accessing water reserves in the soil. Grapevines thrive in well-drained soils and are responsive to variations in climate and topography, allowing for diverse expressions of flavor in wine production. Olive trees, with their evergreen foliage and slow growth, can survive in marginal soils where annual crops might fail, and they exhibit remarkable longevity, with some specimens living for centuries.  

**Economic Importance**  
Throughout history, the economic value of grapes and olives has been multifaceted. Wine and olive oil served as both dietary staples and luxury goods, fueling commerce and taxation systems in ancient empires. In Roman times, estates dedicated to viticulture and olive cultivation were common, and both products were exported across the empire. In the medieval period, monastic communities maintained vineyards and olive groves, preserving agricultural knowledge during times of political instability.  

Modern Mediterranean economies continue to rely heavily on these crops. Countries such as Spain, Italy, Greece, and France are among the largest producers of wine and olive oil globally. These industries support rural livelihoods, contribute to tourism through wine routes and olive festivals, and generate significant export revenues.  

**Role in Traditional Cuisine**  
The culinary traditions of the Mediterranean are inseparable from grapes and olives. Olive oil serves as a primary cooking fat and flavoring agent, integral to dishes from simple salads to complex stews. Grapes are consumed fresh, dried as raisins, or transformed into wine, which often accompanies meals and is used in cooking. Regional variations reflect local terroirs and cultural preferences: robust red wines in southern Italy, delicate whites in coastal Greece, and distinctive olive oils ranging from the peppery varieties of Tuscany to the mild, fruity oils of Andalusia.  

**Cultural Significance**  
Beyond their economic and culinary roles, grapes and olives hold symbolic and ritual importance. In ancient Greece, the olive tree was sacred to Athena, and wine played a central role in religious ceremonies and social gatherings. The olive branch became a universal symbol of peace, while wine’s association with celebration and community persists in contemporary Mediterranean societies.  

**Sustainability and Modern Practices**  
In recent decades, there has been renewed emphasis on sustainable practices in perennial crop cultivation. Organic viticulture and olive farming are increasingly common, with attention to soil health, biodiversity, and reduced chemical inputs. Traditional methods such as dry farming—relying on natural rainfall rather than irrigation—are being revisited as climate change intensifies water scarcity in the region. Agroforestry models incorporating olives and grapes with other perennial species are also emerging, blending ancient wisdom with modern ecological science.  

**Conclusion**  
The historical cultivation of grapes and olives in the Mediterranean reflects a long-standing synergy between environmental conditions, human ingenuity, and cultural expression. Their continued prominence in agriculture and cuisine underscores their enduring value, not only as economic assets but as living symbols of Mediterranean heritage. As global interest in sustainable food systems grows, the lessons embedded in these perennial crops offer guidance for balancing productivity with ecological stewardship.

## Gas Pressure and the Installation & Operation of Natural Gas/Propane Fireplaces Establishing correct gas pressure is critical to the successful installation and safe operation of a residential fireplace. Incorrect pressure can lead to poor performance at best, and damage to the unit in a worst case scenario. Gas pressure is measured as the force the gas exerts on the walls of its container. In this case, the container is the gas line to the fireplace. Measure line pressure with a manometer, which reads pressure as inches of water column (inch WC) or in millibars (MB). One pound of gas pressure measures as 28″ WC pressure. !Comparison between a digital and an analog manometer ## The Consequences of Incorrect Gas Pressure If gas pressure to the fireplace is too low, it can cause a weak pilot flame, very small burner flames, and annoying drop outs. If the pressure is too high, it can damage the gas valve. Therefore, robust flames, quiet operation, and longevity of fireplace components is reliant on establishing correct gas pressure. ## **Nominal Operating Pressure for Residential Fireplaces** Nominal operating pressure for a gas fireplace depends on the type of fuel being used. While a Propane system operates at a true ½ lb or 14″ WC, natural gas operates at ¼ lb or 7″ WC but is still referred to as ½ lb. ### **Natural Gas** Residential gas is delivered to the meter at high pressure, then reduced to ½ lb pressure to supply appliances in the building. **Operating Gas Pressure:** 7″ WC (minimum) to 5.5″ WC (maximum) **Manifold Pressure:** 3.5″ WC ### Propane The gas leaving the tank in a propane system is usually very high pressure. The regulator at the tank will reduce pressure to around 2lb or 56″ WC, which is still too high for a fireplace. Therefore, it will require the installation of an adjustable ½ lb regulator. **Operating Gas Pressure:** 11″ WC (minimum) to 14″ WC (maximum) **Manifold Pressure:** 10″ WC

Human-powered equipment is occasionally used to generate, and sometimes to store, electrical energy for use where no other source of power is available. These include the Gibson girl survival radio, wind-up or (clockwork) radio and pedal radio. ## Available power \ [edit\] Normal human metabolism produces heat at a basal metabolic rate of around 80 watts.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_power?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-1) During a bicycle race, an elite cyclist can produce around 440 watts of mechanical power over an hour and track cyclists in short bursts over 2500 watts; modern racing bicycles have greater than 95% mechanical efficiency. An adult of good fitness is more likely to average between 50 and 150 watts for an hour of vigorous exercise.\ _[clarification needed_\] Over an 8-hour work shift, an average, healthy, well-fed and motivated manual laborer may sustain an output of around 75 watts of power "Power (physics)").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_power?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-2) However, the potential yield of human electric power is decreased by the inefficiency of any generator device, since all real generators incur losses during the energy conversion process.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_power?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_power?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-4) It is possible to use exercise equipment for power generation, by attaching the moving parts to components of electric generators;[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_power?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-sweatinto-5) some home gym equipment uses DC generators to power readouts, displays, and control the amount of resistance offered by the machine.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_power?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-sweatinto-5) The amount of energy generated is so small compared to industrial power sources that the cost of conversion equipment makes it financially impractical.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_power?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-sweatinto-5) For example, supplying an average United States home solely with electricity generated from exercise equipment for one day would require more than a hundred people to ride stationary bicycles for all of it.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_power?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-sweatinto-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_power?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-6) ## Transport \ [edit\] Main article: Human-powered transport [](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:WTF_Josh_Bluntschli_Bike_rider.jpg) Bicycles are an example of human-powered transportation. Several forms of transport utilize human power. They include the bicycle, wheelchair, walking, skateboard, wheelbarrow, rowing, skis, and rickshaw. Some forms may utilize more than one person. The historical galley was propelled by freemen or citizens in ancient times, and by slaves captured by pirates in more recent times. The MacCready Gossamer Condor was the first human-powered aircraft capable of controlled and sustained flight, making its first flight in 1977. In 2007, Jason Lewis "Jason Lewis (adventurer)") of Expedition 360 became the first person to circumnavigate the globe at non-polar latitudes using only human power—walking, biking, and rollerblading across the landmasses; and swimming, kayaking, rowing, and using a 26-foot-long pedal-powered boat to cross the oceans.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_power?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_power?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-8) ## General devices and machines \ [edit\] [](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Coldbath-fields-treadmill-mayhew-p306.jpg) A penal treadwheel used at the Coldbath Fields Prison in London, England in 1864[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Shaking_Torch.jpg) A mechanically powered flashlight. This uses a linear generator and is charged by shaking along its long axis. Treadwheels, also called treadmills, are engines or machines powered by humans. These may resemble a water wheel in appearance, and can be worked either by a human treading paddles set into its circumference (treadmill), or by a human standing inside it (treadwheel). Some devices use human power. They may directly use mechanical power#Mechanical_power "Power (physics)") from muscles, or a generator may convert energy generated by the body into electrical power. Human-powered equipment primarily consists of electrical appliances which can be powered by electricity generated by human muscle power as an alternative to conventional sources of electricity such as disposable primary batteries and the electrical grid. Such devices contain electric generators or an induction system to recharge their batteries. Separate crank-operated generators are now available to recharge battery-powered portable electronic devices such as mobile phones. Others, such as mechanically powered flashlights, have the generator integrated within the device. Wrist watches can use muscle power to keep their mainsprings wound up. An alternative to rechargeable batteries for electricity storage is supercapacitors, now being used in some devices such as the mechanically powered flashlight shown here. Devices that store the energy mechanically, rather than electrically, include clockwork radios with a mainspring, which is wound up by a crank and turns a generator to power the radio. An early example of regular use of human-powered electrical equipment is in early telephone systems; current to ring the remote bell was provided by a subscriber cranking a handle on the telephone, which turned a small magneto generator. Human-powered devices are useful as emergency equipment, when natural disaster, war, or civil disturbance make regular power supplies unavailable. They have also been seen as economical for use in poor countries, where batteries may be expensive and mains electricity unreliable or unavailable. They are also an environmentally preferable alternative to the use of disposable batteries, which are a wasteful source of energy and may introduce heavy metals into the environment. Communication is a common application for the relatively small amount of electric power that can be generated by a human turning a generator. ## Human-powered radio \ [edit\] | | | | --- | --- | | | It has been suggested that this section be **split** out into another article. ( **Discuss**) _(December 2020)_ | ### Survival radio \ [edit\] [](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GibsonGirlSurvivalRadio.agr.jpg) BC-778 "Gibson Girl" radio transmitter The World War II-era Gibson girl survival radio used a hand-cranked generator to provide power; this avoided the unreliable performance of dry-cell batteries that might be stored for months before they were needed, although it had the drawback that the survivor had to be fit enough to turn the crank. Survival radios were invented and deployed by both sides during the war.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_power?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-9) The SCR-578 (and the similar post-war AN/CRT-3) survival radio transmitters carried by aircraft on over-water operations were given the nickname " Gibson Girl" because of their "hourglass" shape, which allowed them to be held stationary between the legs while the generator handle was turned.\ _[citation needed_\] ### Military radio \ [edit\] [](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:US_shore_patrol_group_operating_Signal_Corps_radios.jpg) U.S. soldiers using a GN-45 hand crank generator to power their radio set during World War II During World War II, U.S. troops sometimes employed hand crank generators, GN-35 and GN-45, to power Signal Corps Radio transmitter/receivers.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_power?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-10) The hand cranking was laborious, but generated sufficient current for smaller radio sets, such as the SCR-131, SCR-161, SCR-171, SCR-284, and SCR-694.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_power?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-ThompsonHarris1966-11) ### Windup radio \ [edit\] [](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Clockwork_Radio.JPG) The original Baygen clockwork radio with crank in winding position A **windup radio** or **clockwork radio** is a radio that is powered by human muscle power rather than batteries or the electrical grid. In the most common arrangement, an internal electric generator is run by a mainspring, which is wound by a hand crank "Crank (mechanism)") on the case. Turning the crank winds the spring and a full winding will allow several hours of operation. Alternatively, the generator can charge an internal battery.\ _[citation needed_\] Radios powered by handcranked generators are not new, but their market was previously seen as limited to emergency or military organizations. The modern clockwork radio was designed and patented in 1991 by British inventor Trevor Baylis as a response to the HIV/AIDS crisis. He envisioned it as a radio for use by poor people in developing countries, especially in Africa, without access to batteries. In 1994, British accountant Chris Staines and his South African partner, Rory Stear, secured the worldwide license to the invention and cofounded Baygen Power Industries (now Freeplay Energy Ltd), which produced the first commercial model. The key to its design, which is no longer in use, was the use of a constant-velocity spring "Spring (device)") to store the potential energy. After Baylis lost control of his invention when Baygen became Freeplay, the Freeplay Energy units switched to disposable batteries charged by cheaper hand-crank generators.\ _[citation needed_\] Like other self-powered equipment, windup radios were intended for camping, emergencies and for areas where there is no electrical grid and replacement batteries are hard to obtain, such as in developing countries or remote settlements. They are also useful where a radio is not used on a regular basis and batteries would deteriorate, such as at a vacation house or cabin.\ _[citation needed_\] Windup radios designed for emergency use often include flashlights, blinking emergency lights, and emergency sirens. They also may include multiple alternate power sources, such as disposable or rechargeable batteries, cigarette lighter receptacles, and solar cells.\ _[citation needed_\] ## Pedal-powered transmitter \ [edit\] [](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Solitary_Island_Pedal_Radio_br_3.jpg) Pedal radio being used in South Solitary Island lighthouse, to communicate with Norah Head Lightstation, 1946 The **pedal radio** (or **pedal wireless**) was a radio transmitter-receiver powered by a pedal-driven generator. It was developed by South Australian engineer and inventor Alfred Traeger in 1929 as a way of providing radio communications to remote homesteads "Homestead (buildings)") and cattle stations in the Australian outback.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_power?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-12) There were no mains or generator power available at the time and batteries to provide the power required would have been too expensive. It was a highly important invention,[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_power?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-NLA-13) as it was this technology that enabled the Royal Flying Doctor Service, and later the School of the Air, linking people living remotely to emergency services and education.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_power?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-14)

**Cutting Energy Costs at Home: Practical Strategies for Lasting Savings**  

As energy prices continue to rise and households look for ways to reduce monthly expenses, making smart changes to how a home consumes energy can yield significant savings. Fortunately, many of these strategies not only lower utility bills but also enhance comfort and extend the lifespan of household systems. In this post, we’ll explore how improving insulation, upgrading appliances, and optimizing thermostat use can make a tangible difference.  

---

### 1. Insulation: The Foundation of Energy Efficiency  

One of the most effective ways to reduce energy costs is to prevent wasted heating and cooling. Poor insulation allows conditioned air to escape and outside temperatures to seep in, forcing heating and cooling systems to work harder.  

**Attic and Wall Insulation**  
The attic is often the biggest culprit when it comes to heat loss in winter and heat gain in summer. Adding or upgrading insulation here can dramatically improve energy performance. For walls, especially in older homes, blown-in insulation can fill gaps without major renovations.  

**Windows and Doors**  
Weatherstripping and caulking around windows and doors can seal air leaks. Double- or triple-pane windows provide better thermal resistance than single-pane alternatives, and storm doors can add an extra layer of protection against drafts.  

By enhancing insulation, homeowners can stabilize indoor temperatures, reduce reliance on heating and cooling systems, and see immediate reductions in energy consumption.  

---

### 2. Energy-Efficient Appliances: Long-Term Savings Through Smart Investments  

Appliances account for a substantial portion of a home’s electricity use. Upgrading to energy-efficient models, particularly those certified by programs such as ENERGY STAR, can lower operating costs without sacrificing performance.  

**Refrigerators and Freezers**  
Older units often consume far more electricity than modern equivalents. New models use advanced compressors and better insulation to keep food fresh while minimizing energy draw.  

**Washers and Dryers**  
High-efficiency washers use less water and require less energy for heating, while modern dryers often feature moisture sensors that prevent over-drying.  

**Lighting**  
Switching from incandescent bulbs to LED lighting is one of the easiest changes to make. LEDs last longer, consume a fraction of the energy, and produce less heat, which can also reduce cooling costs in warmer climates.  

Though the upfront cost of upgrading appliances can be higher, the savings on monthly utility bills and the reduced environmental impact make these investments worthwhile.  

---

### 3. Thermostat Optimization: Precision Control for Comfort and Savings  

Heating and cooling systems are among the largest energy consumers in a home. By controlling them more efficiently, homeowners can cut costs without compromising comfort.  

**Programmable Thermostats**  
These devices allow users to set temperature schedules that align with daily routines, lowering heating or cooling output when the home is empty or occupants are asleep.  

**Smart Thermostats**  
Smart models go a step further, learning household patterns and adjusting settings automatically. Many can be controlled remotely via smartphone apps, enabling adjustments on the go.  

**Zoned Heating and Cooling**  
If the home’s HVAC system supports it, zoning allows different areas to be heated or cooled independently. This means unused rooms aren’t consuming energy unnecessarily.  

Even small adjustments—such as lowering the heat by a few degrees in winter or raising the cooling set point in summer—can add up to substantial savings over time.  

---

### Putting It All Together  

Reducing energy costs in residential homes is not about making one big change but rather combining multiple strategies for cumulative impact. Insulating effectively keeps conditioned air where it belongs, energy-efficient appliances ensure less waste during everyday tasks, and thermostat optimization fine-tunes climate control to match actual needs.  

Homeowners who take a systematic approach—starting with an energy audit to identify the biggest inefficiencies—can prioritize upgrades for maximum benefit. Over time, these changes will not only lower utility bills but also improve overall comfort and resilience against fluctuating energy prices.  

With thoughtful planning and targeted investments, any household can transform its energy profile, achieving lasting savings while making the home a more pleasant place to live.

## Overview Dioxins are environmental pollutants. They belong to the so-called dirty dozen – a group of dangerous chemicals known as persistent organic pollutants (POPs). Dioxins are of concern because of their highly toxic potential. Experiments have shown they affect several organs and systems. Once dioxins enter the body, they last a long time because of their chemical stability and their ability to be absorbed by fat tissue, where they are then stored in the body. Their half-life in the body is estimated to be 7 to 11 years. In the environment, dioxins tend to accumulate in the food chain. The higher an animal is in the food chain, the higher the concentration of dioxins. The chemical name for dioxin is 2,3,7,8- tetrachlorodibenzo para dioxin (TCDD). The name dioxins is often used for the family of structurally and chemically related _polychlorinated dibenzo para dioxins (PCDDs)_ and _polychlorinated dibenzofurans (PCDFs)._ Certain dioxin-like polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) with similar toxic properties are also included under the term dioxins. Some 419 types of dioxin-related compounds have been identified but only about 30 of these are considered to have significant toxicity, with TCDD being the most toxic. ## Sources of contamination Dioxins are mainly by-products of industrial processes but can also result from natural processes, such as volcanic eruptions and forest fires. They are unwanted by-products of many manufacturing processes including smelting, chlorine bleaching of paper pulp and the manufacture of some herbicides and pesticides. Uncontrolled waste incinerators (solid waste and hospital waste) are often the worst culprits of environmental release due to incomplete burning. Technology is available that allows for controlled waste incineration with low dioxin emissions. Although formation of dioxins is local, environmental distribution is global. The highest levels are found in some soils, sediments and food, especially dairy products, meat, fish and shellfish. Very low levels are found in plants, water and air. Extensive stores of PCB-based waste industrial oils, many with high levels of PCDFs, exist throughout the world. Long-term storage and improper disposal of this material may result in dioxin release into the environment and the contamination of human and animal food supplies. PCB-based waste is not easily disposed of without contamination of the environment and human populations. Such material needs to be treated as hazardous waste and is best destroyed by high temperature incineration in specialized facilities. ## Effects on human health Short-term exposure of humans to high levels of dioxins may result in skin lesions, such as chloracne and patchy darkening of the skin, and altered liver function. Long-term exposure is linked to impairment of the immune system, the developing nervous system, the endocrine system and reproductive functions. Chronic exposure of animals to dioxins has resulted in several types of cancer. TCDD was evaluated by the WHO’s International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) in 1997 and 2012. Based on animal and human epidemiology data, TCDD was classified by IARC as a known human carcinogen. However, TCDD does not affect genetic material and there is a level of exposure below which cancer risk would be negligible. Due to the omnipresence of dioxins, all people have background exposure and a certain level of dioxins in the body, leading to the so-called body burden. Current normal background exposure is not expected to affect human health on average. However, due to the high toxic potential of this class of compounds, efforts are needed to reduce current background exposure. The developing fetus is most sensitive to dioxin exposure. Newborns, with rapidly developing organ systems, may also be more vulnerable to certain effects. Some people or groups of people may be exposed to higher levels of dioxins because of their diet (such as high consumers of fish in certain parts of the world) or their occupation (such as workers in the pulp and paper industry, in incineration plants, and at hazardous waste sites). ## Prevention and control Proper incineration of contaminated material is the best available method of preventing and controlling exposure to dioxins. It can also destroy PCB-based waste oils. The incineration process requires temperatures over 850 °C. For the destruction of large amounts of contaminated material, temperatures of 1000 °C or more are required.

Businesses and consumers misconstrue what biodegradation means and how it differs from composting and recycling, which creates issues with labeling and ultimately disposal. All compostable plastics are biodegradable. However, not all biodegradable plastics are compostable. In order to be labeled as compostable, bioplastics must biodegrade in a specified time period leaving no toxins in the soil. Some traditional plastics claim to be oxo-degradable; however, these materials are designed to degrade into smaller and smaller fragments of plastic, which can contaminate soil and waters for years. All compostable plastics are biodegradable. However, not all biodegradable plastics are compostable. Truly biodegradable plastics undergo biodegradation by naturally occurring microorganisms, which help the material degrade into organic matter. Biodegradation refers to anaerobic or aerobic degradation of materials by microorganisms. Depending on the environmental factors (i.e., moisture and temperature), the process will result in carbon dioxide, water, biomass, minerals salts and / or methane. Anaerobic biodegradation occurs without oxygen, meaning that anaerobic microorganisms are dominant, resulting in the production of methane. Conversely, aerobic biodegradation occurs with oxygen, meaning that aerobes are present and use cellular respiration, which produces oxygen and carbon dioxide. Composting is a specific process for biodegradation where aerobes digest organic waste to create compost. We will specifically discuss composting in industrial facilities where the process is carefully controlled because the proper levels of heat, water and soil need to be present, so the proper microorganisms can digest the materials at a consistent rate without leaving toxic residue. “ Biodegradation Bioplastics, as a general category, are plastics that are made from renewable biomass or can biodegrade at the end of their lifecycle. Some bioplastics have both attributes, some only one. For example, there are bio-based plastics that are not biodegradable (e.g., bio-based PET) and petroleum-based plastics that are (e.g., PBAT, PCL). To be truly labeled biodegradable, the plastic must degrade into carbon dioxide, water, biomass and / or mineral salts when exposed to air, moisture and microbes. The materials should not be toxic to the environment. Bio-based materials may also be used as fillers, reinforcements for other biodegradable plastic polymers. In the United States, the plastic needs to be certified compostable, meaning that it needs to comply with ASTM D6400 as certified by a third party organization such as the Biodegradable Products Institute. Thus, the term “certified compostable” is more specific than “biodegradable.” All materials are biodegradable given enough time, but claiming a product is “compostable” denotes that it meets requirements of ASTM D6400 or will degrade 90% in 180 days under the specific humidity, temperature and aeration conditions of an industrial composting facility. The mechanism for biodegradation Biodegradation can occur under aerobic or anaerobic conditions. Carbon dioxide is produced under aerobic conditions while the same materials will produce methane under anaerobic conditions (i.e., landfills). The environment or medium in which a plastic is disposed of will affect the possibility and rate of biodegradation. A biodegradable plastic contains polymers that can be broken down and digested by polymer-degrading microbes in (ideally) aerobic environments where methane isn’t a byproduct. If key environmental factors such as temperature and moisture align, then enough microorganisms can adhere to the surface of the plastic, ingest it and enzymatically degrade it. The mechanism varies between aerobic and anaerobic processes and where the process takes place (e.g., landfill, marine environment or backyard). In general, enzymatic digestion is facilitated by hydrolysis, a two-step process where an enzyme first binds to the ingested polymer to catalyze hydrolytic cleavage. The polymer is then “cleaved” down to molecules with lower molecular weights that are then mineralized to carbon dioxide, water and biomass. Rates of biodegradation Biodegradation rates are influenced by the bioactivity of the location, temperature and moisture levels. The disposal site needs to have an environment conducive to the microorganisms needed to break down the plastic, as most biodegradable polymers degrade faster in significantly hot and wet environments. However, for a biodegradable plastic to properly break down into environmentally friendly components, it needs to be disposed properly. For example, a biodegradable plastic bag thrown into a hedge will take years to properly degrade and even a banana peel needs a minimum of one year. Unfortunately, many biodegradable plastics are improperly discarded in areas that have undesirable environmental conditions, meaning that the products either slowly or never degrade.

plasma ](/wiki/Plasma_\(physics\) "Plasma \(physics\)") arc is generated by
the disintegration and rapid [ spring ](/wiki/Spring_\(device\) "Spring
\(device\)") -loaded separation of the fusible element, which is typically a
specialized metal rod that passes through a compressed mass of boric acid
within the fuse assembly. The high-temperature plasma causes the boric acid to
rapidly decompose into [ water vapor ](/wiki/Water_vapor "Water vapor") and [
boric anhydride ](/wiki/Boron_trioxide "Boron trioxide") , and in-turn, the
vaporization products de-ionize the plasma, helping to interrupt the
electrical fault.  [41]

Officials responsible for mosquito control programs make decisions to use pesticides based on an evaluation of the risks to the general public from diseases transmitted by mosquitoes or on an evaluation of the nuisance level that communities can tolerate from a mosquito infestation. Based on surveillance and monitoring, mosquito control officials select specific pesticides and other control measures that best suit local conditions in order to achieve effective control of mosquitoes with the least impact on human health and the environment. It is especially important to conduct effective mosquito prevention programs by eliminating breeding habitats or applying pesticides to control the early life stages of the mosquito. Prevention programs, such as elimination of any standing water that could serve as a breeding site, help reduce the adult mosquito population and the need to apply other pesticides for adult mosquito control. Since no pesticide can be considered $1 0 0 %$ safe, pesticide applicators and the general public should always exercise care and follow specified safety precautions during use to reduce risks. This fact sheet provides basic information on larvicides, a type of pesticide used in mosquito control programs. # What are Larvicides? The mosquito goes through four distinct stages during its life cycle: egg, larva, pupa, and adult (see box). Larvicides kill insect larvae. Larvicides include biological insecticides, such as the microbial larvicides Bacillus sphaericus and Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis. Larvicides include other chemicals used for controlling mosquito larvae, such as temephos, methoprene, oils, and monomolecular films. Larvicide treatment of breeding habitats help reduce the adult mosquito population in nearby areas. larvicides are used as one of several tools in mosquito control # How are Larvicides Used in Mosquito Control? State and local agencies in charge of mosquito control typically employ a variety of techniques in an Integrated Pest Management (IPM) approach, which include surveillance, source reduction, larviciding and adulticiding, to control mosquito populations. Since mosquitoes must have water to breed, source reduction aims to cut down opportunities for breeding, and can be as simple as turning over trapped water in a container to large-scale engineering and management of marsh water. Larviciding involves applying chemicals to habitats to kill pre-adult mosquitoes. Larviciding can reduce overall pesticide usage in a control program by reducing or eliminating the need for ground or aerial application of chemicals to kill adult mosquitoes. microbial larvicides are bacteria that are registered as pesticides # What are Microbial Larvicides? Microbial larvicides are bacteria that are registered as pesticides for control of mosquito larvae in outdoor areas such as irrigation ditches, flood water, standing ponds, woodland pools, pastures, tidal water, fresh or saltwater marshes, and storm water retention areas. Duration of effectiveness depends primarily on the mosquito species, the environmental conditions, the formulation of the product, and water quality. Microbial larvicides may be used along with other mosquito control measures in an integrated pest management (IPM) program. The microbial larvicides used for mosquito control are Bacillus **Mosquito Life Cycle** egg - hatch when exposed to water; larva - (pl. - larvae) lives in the water; molts several times; most species surface to breathe air; pupa - (pl. - pupae) non-feeding stage just prior to emerging as adult; adult - flies short time after emerging and after its body parts have hardened. thuringiensis israelensis (Bti) and Bacillus sphaericus (Bs). microbial larvicides are harmful to insects but not mammals Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis (Bti) is a naturally occurring soil bacterium registered for control of mosquito larvae. Bti was first registered by EPA as an insecticide in 1983. Mosquito larvae eat the Bti product which is made up of the dormant spore form of the bacterium and an associated pure toxin. The toxin disrupts the gut in the mosquito by binding to receptor cells present in insects, but not in mammals. There are $2 5 Bti$ products registered for use in the United States. Aquabac, Teknar, Vectobac, and LarvX are examples of common trade names for the mosquito control products. Bacillus sphaericus is a naturally occurring bacterium that is found throughout the world. Bacillus sphaericus was initially registered by EPA in 1991 for use against various kinds of mosquito larvae. Mosquito larvae ingest the bacteria, and as with Bti , the toxin disrupts the gut in the mosquito by binding to receptor cells present in insects, but not in mammals. VectoLex CG and WDG are registered B. sphaericus products, and are effective for approximately one to four weeks after application. microbial larvicides do not pose concerns for human health or the environment when used according to product labels # Do Microbial Larvicides Pose Risks to Human Health? The microbial pesticides have undergone extensive testing prior to registration. They are essentially nontoxic to humans, so there are no concerns for human health effects with Bti , or B. sphaericus, when they are used according to label directions. # Do Microbial Larvicides Pose Risks to Wildlife or the Environment? Extensive testing shows that microbial larvicides do not pose risks to wildlife, non-target species or the environment.

Pedalling a modern stationary bicycle to produce electricity might be a great work-out, but in many cases, it is not sustainable. While humans are rather inefficient engines converting food into work, this is not the problem we want to address here; people have to move in order to stay healthy, so we might as well use that energy to operate machinery. The trouble is that the present approach to pedal power results in highly inefficient machines. > When operating a bicycle generator you are basically pedalling to produce the energy required to manufacture the battery. There are two ways to power a device by pedalling. You can power it directly through a mechanical connection - as was the case with all pedal powered machines for sale at the turn of the 20th century. Or, you can pedal to generate electricity, which is then used to power the device. In the 1970s, most research was aimed at direct mechanical power transmission. Today, the interest in pedal powered machines is almost exclusively aimed at generating electricity, for instance for charging cell phones and laptops - products that did not even exist in the 1970s. With one exception (the ‘ Fender Blender’, a pedalled powered machine to make smoothies), the only pedal powered machinery that is now commercially available in the western world (offered by Windstream, Convergence Tech and Magnificent Revolution) are stands to fit your bike to, connected to an electric motor/generator and a battery. That is a combination that can quickly convert your regular road bicycle into an electricity generator. These are also the pedal powered machines which are used for educational and arts projects, like powering a music concert, a cinema projection or a supercomputer, or teaching kids the difference in energy use between, for instance, an incandescent light bulb and an energy saving lamp. In an effort to raise awareness about energy use and global warming, the BBC even made a TV-programme in which an entire household was powered via these generators, with 80 cyclists generating up to 14 kW. These multi-person pedal power generators were pioneered in the 1970s by the Campus Center for Appropriate Technology (CCAT). ## Generating electricity is very inefficient There are several problems with the present-day approach to pedal power. First of all, it is important to know that generating electricity is far from the most efficient way to apply pedal power, due to the internal energy losses in the battery, the battery management system, other electronic parts, and the motor/generator. These energy losses add up quickly: 10 to 35 percent in the battery, 10 to 20 percent in the motor/generator and 5 to 15 percent in the converter (which converts direct current to alternate current). (Sources: 1/ 2/ 3). The energy loss in the voltage regulator (or DC to DC converter, which prevents you from blowing up the battery) is about 25 percent (sources: 1/ 2). This means that the total energy loss in a pedal powered generator will be 42 to 67.5 percent (calculation example for highest loss: 100 watt input = 80 watt after 20% loss in motor/generator = 57.5 watts after 25% energy loss in voltage regulator = 37.5 watts after 35% loss in battery = 32.5 watts after 15% loss in converter = 32.5 watts output = efficiency of 32.5% or energy loss of 67.5%). > You have to pedal 2 to 3 times as hard or as long if you choose to power a device via electricity compared to powering the same device mechanically Furthermore, there will be an additional slight loss as the battery stands idle, and the charge efficiency (also known as “charge acceptance” or “coulombic efficiency”) of the battery will deteriorate over time. And to make the calculation complete, you should actually also include the energy loss in the electrical device that you are powering (we won’t do that here). An energy loss of 42 to 67.5 percent of naturally means that it takes 42 to 67.5 percent more effort or time to power a device (say, a blender) via electricity compared to powering the same device mechanically. This can be considered an acceptable loss if you are using solar panels or a wind turbine connected to a battery as an energy source, but it becomes rather problematic when you have to deliver the energy yourself. If you produce 100 watts of power and 42 to 67.5 percent is lost in the conversion, there is only 32.5 to 58 watts left to power the device. If you power the same device mechanically, you deliver 100 watts straight to it. You thus have to pedal 2 to 3 times as hard or as long if you choose to take the intermediate step of generating electricity and storing it in a battery.
